M’Chigeeng First Nation

M’Chigeeng First Nation’s public education materials offer a starting path through Anishinaabemowin learning and community schooling. The sources explain how recorded speech, teaching resources and relationships among learners, families and Elders support learning; they do not constitute a full community history.

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

Learning from recorded speech

M’Chigeeng’s Anishinaabemowin Revival Program describes digitizing earlier community television recordings alongside interviews with Elders. Its public introduction explains that Ojibwe transcripts and word glossaries support learners working with natural speech. This guide points readers to that community-led method; it does not claim the linked recordings have been watched or translate their teachings.

Read the sources [1] M’Chigeeng First Nation

02

School, family and community relationships

In Lakeview School’s 2026–2027 handbook, interim principal Deana Debassige-Wood emphasizes belonging, culturally responsive learning and relationships with families, Elders and Knowledge Keepers. The opening pages also explain how learning periods, nutrition and physical activity are arranged. These are the school’s stated educational commitments for that year, not independently measured outcomes.

Read the sources [2] Lakeview School / M’Chigeeng First Nation
